canonicalExplanation.summary: Headings `<h1>`–`<h6>` build the page's **outline**, like a book's table of contents. Use **one** descriptive `h1` for the page's main subject, `h2` for its main sections, `h3` for sub-sections inside an h2, and so on — don't skip levels downward. Choose a heading level for its **place in the outline**, never for its font size; CSS controls size.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Screen-reader users often jump from heading to heading to skim a page, the way you glance at bold titles. If your headings are chosen for looks — an h4 because it's "the right size" — that outline becomes nonsense. A page uses one descriptive h1 for its main subject and h2 elements for peer sections such as syllabus and schedule. In this lesson you'll create and review a logical heading hierarchy for a multi-section page.

Use h2 and style it smaller with CSS."], "answer": 1, "why": "Level expresses structure. CSS can make an h2 any size you want."}

sections.body: You should know the **Standards-mode document skeleton** — headings go inside body.

``` | Rule | Why | |---|---| | one descriptive h1. | says what the whole page is about. | | peer sections share a level. | Syllabus, Schedule, Contact are all h2. | | don't skip down (h2 → h4). | the outline would have a missing level. | | level ≠ size. | style size with CSS. | ```reveal {"prompt": "Can you go from an h3 back up to an h2?", "answer": "Yes. Going **up** any number of levels is fine — it starts a new higher-level section. Only skipping **down** leaves gaps."} ```

sections.heading: Read the outline

includes: Build a heading outline with one h1 and properly nested h2–h6.
Review a page's headings for skipped levels and size-driven choices.
excludes: The sectioning outline algorithm (never implemented by browsers).

outcomes: Create and review a logical heading hierarchy for a multi-section page.

examples.title: A course page outline
examples.situation: A page uses one descriptive h1 for its main subject and h2 elements for peer sections such as syllabus and schedule.
walkthrough: **One descriptive h1:** "Web Basics — Autumn Course" names the main subject.
**Peer sections as h2:** Syllabus, Schedule and Contact are siblings, so all are h2.
**Sub-sections as h3:** each week inside Syllabus is an h3 — no levels skipped, so the browser can build a clean outline.
examples.result: A screen reader's heading list reads like a clear table of contents for the course page.

examples.title: The size-driven headings
examples.situation: A blog post uses `<h1>` for the site name, `<h1>` for the title, and `<h4>` for sections "because h2 looked too big".
walkthrough: Two h1s make the main subject unclear.
Jumping from h1 to h4 leaves gaps in the outline.
Fix: one h1 for the post title, h2 for sections, and CSS for sizes; the site name can be plain text or a logo link.
examples.result: The outline becomes post title → sections, and the design still looks right via CSS.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Heading elements should be chosen by the font size the design needs.
misconceptions.correction: Heading levels describe the document outline: one h1 for the main subject, then nested levels without skipping downward. Visual size is a CSS decision that can be applied to any level.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The size-driven headings", which two outline problems appeared?

analogy.example: Headings are like a **book's table of contents**: Book title (h1), chapters (h2), sections within chapters (h3). You wouldn't number a section 4.1.1.1 directly under chapter 4.
usefulFor: seeing size as separate from structure
limitations: Books have fixed layouts; the same HTML outline can be styled many ways.
Web pages are often skimmed by heading navigation, not read front to back.

steps.explanation: The page uses one descriptive h1 for its main subject.
Syllabus is an h2 section with an h3 sub-section inside.
Schedule is another h2, a peer of the syllabus section.

trace.textAlternative: Building a heading outline. Step 1, Main subject: h1 is Web Basics — Autumn Course. The page uses one descriptive h1 for its main subject. remediation.explanation: List only your headings, indented by level. If the list doesn't read like a sensible table of contents, fix the levels — then fix the look with CSS.
remediation.retryPrompt: Make the list for "The size-driven headings".

recap.summary: To create a logical heading hierarchy, use one descriptive h1, give peer sections the same level, nest sub-sections one level deeper without skipping down, and choose levels by outline position — never by font size.
retrievalPrompts: How many h1s should a page usually have?
Is it OK to jump from h2 to h4?
